passage:
"Nani, Nani!" Zeenat toddled in holding a wooden duck.
"What have you got, jaan?" asked Tanuja Nani.
"Duck! Look!" Zeenat pushed it into her lap.
"Such a fine duck!"
Zeenat held half her biscuit to Nani's mouth. "You eat."
"For me? Thank you, my love."
Then Zeenat bumped her head on the table leg, wailed and reached up both arms. Nani lifted her and rocked. Soon Zeenat wriggled down and went back to the duck.

qa.q: What toy did Zeenat show Tanuja Nani?
qa.a: A wooden duck.

qa.q: What does Zeenat reaching up both arms after bumping her head suggest she expects?
qa.a: She expects Nani to pick her up and comfort her, because she trusts Nani to be there.

qa.q: Which moment shows Nani's comfort working, and what could Nani keep doing?
qa.a: After Nani rocked her, Zeenat soon wriggled down and went back to the duck. Nani can keep giving quick, warm comfort so Zeenat feels safe to play again.

qa.q: What is it like for Tanuja Nani when Zeenat holds half the biscuit to her mouth?
qa.a: It is likely touching for Nani, a small gift of trust and love from the toddler ❤️

grounding: A reliably comforted toddler shows a toy, shares food and seeks a hug from a trusted grandmother, then goes back to play.

passage:
Daycare note, Tuesday. Arnab (2 years). Written by Gopika.
Arrived teary and came straight to me for a long hug. At snack time he pushed an apple slice into my hand. Twice he brought me the red truck just to show it, waited for my "Wow!" and ran back. Woke from nap upset and settled quickly on my lap.
Next: I'll keep greeting him at the gate this week and tell his mother how quickly he settles now 🙂

qa.q: What did Arnab bring Gopika twice?
qa.a: The red truck, just to show it.

qa.q: Why do you think Arnab waited for Gopika's "Wow!" before running back?
qa.a: He wanted Gopika to share his excitement, and the reply made him feel safe and confident enough to go back and play.

qa.q: What is wise about Gopika's plan to greet Arnab at the gate?
qa.a: Being the same warm person every morning keeps his comfort reliable, which is what lets him settle and explore.

qa.q: How might Arnab's mother feel reading that he settles quickly now?
qa.a: She would probably feel relieved that he trusts his caregiver and manages well away from home.

grounding: A toddler who trusts his caregiver hugs Gopika, shares his apple and shows off his toy, building early closeness.

passage: In the courtyard of their village house, Sonali was sorting wheat when little Mehak, not yet two, waddled over with a fistful of puffed rice. She pushed a few grains into her mother's mouth and laughed. A goat bleated at the gate. Mehak froze, then ran to bury her face in Sonali's dupatta. Sonali stroked her back and hummed. Soon Mehak peeked out, fetched her clay whistle and held it up high for her mother to see.

qa.q: What did Mehak push into her mother's mouth?
qa.a: A few grains of puffed rice.

qa.q: What does Mehak burying her face in Sonali's dupatta suggest she feels?
qa.a: The goat startled her, and she ran to her mother because she feels safe with her and trusts her to comfort her.

qa.q: Which of Sonali's choices helped Mehak go back to playing?
qa.a: Sonali stayed calm, stroked her back and hummed instead of hurrying her, so Mehak felt safe enough to peek out and fetch her whistle.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel when Mehak holds up the clay whistle for her?
qa.a: She would likely feel warm and proud that her daughter wants to share her small treasures with her.

grounding: A toddler who is reliably comforted shares food, runs to her mother when scared and then shows her a toy.

passage: In a small flat in Malmö, Diego, two, woke from his nap crying and padded straight to Mormor Ulla at the table. She lifted him onto her lap, and he pressed his wet cheek into her cardigan until the sobs slowed. Then he wriggled down, fetched his toy tractor and held it up to her face. "Look!" At snack time he broke his rice cake in two and pushed the bigger half into her hand. "Mormor eat."

qa.q: What did Diego push into Mormor Ulla's hand at snack time?
qa.a: He pushed the bigger half of his rice cake into her hand.

qa.q: Why did Diego go straight to Mormor Ulla when he woke up crying?
qa.a: He seems to trust her to comfort him and expects her lap to be a safe place to calm down.

qa.q: How does Mormor Ulla's quick comfort help Diego?
qa.a: By lifting him onto her lap and letting him settle, she shows him closeness is safe, so he comes back to share his toy and food.

qa.q: How might Mormor Ulla feel when Diego gives her the bigger half?
qa.a: She would probably feel touched and loved, seeing his trust and affection in that small gift. 🤍

grounding: A two-year-old who is reliably comforted seeks a hug, shows his toy and shares food with his grandmother, showing early trust.

passage: I'm Shalini, and I live across the landing from little Lalremsiami, who is two. I can't know what goes on in her head, but I notice things. When her father comes up the stairs, she drops whatever she has and runs to him with her arms up. Yesterday she carried her cup of puffed rice to him and fed him one piece at a time, very seriously. When she tripped, she cried only until he picked her up.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami carry to her father?
qa.a: She carried her cup of puffed rice to him.

qa.q: What does Lalremsiami's running with her arms up suggest about how she feels about her father?
qa.a: It suggests she trusts him and feels safe and happy with him, expecting to be picked up.

qa.q: Why does it matter that her crying stopped once her father picked her up?
qa.a: It shows his comfort works for her, and steady comfort like this builds the trust she can carry into closeness later.

qa.q: How does Shalini, watching from across the landing, seem to see this father and child?
qa.a: Shalini seems to see a warm, trusting bond, while admitting it is only a guess from outside.

grounding: A neighbour watches a two-year-old run to her father for hugs and share food with him, showing the trust built by reliable comfort.

passage: In the mud-walled courtyard, two-year-old Pooja tugs at Shalini maasi's dupatta. Maasi has rocked her through every fever and every scraped knee this winter. Pooja holds up a soggy piece of roti and pushes it toward Maasi's mouth, then waits. Maasi takes a tiny bite. "Mmm, thank you!" Pooja giggles, climbs into her lap and presses a sticky cheek to her arm. Then she wriggles down and runs to fetch her clay bullock to show her.

qa.q: What does Pooja fetch to show Shalini maasi?
qa.a: Pooja fetches her clay bullock.

qa.q: What does Pooja's pushing the roti toward Maasi suggest she feels?
qa.a: It suggests Pooja feels safe and affectionate with Maasi, trusting enough to share her food and wait for a reaction.

qa.q: How does Maasi's small bite and "thank you" help Pooja?
qa.a: By accepting the gift warmly, Maasi shows Pooja that reaching out is welcomed, which builds her trust further.

qa.q: What would change if Maasi often pushed Pooja away when she was upset?
qa.a: Pooja might hold back her hugs and gifts, feeling unsure whether closeness would be met with comfort.

grounding: A toddler who has been reliably comforted shares food, seeks hugs and shows toys to a trusted adult.

passage: It is a hot Christmas afternoon in Valparaíso, and the fan hums over the tiles. Noa, not yet two, toddles to her papá, Diego, holding a dripping slice of watermelon in both fists. She pushes it at his chin. He pretends to take a huge bite. Noa squeals, drops the melon and reaches up with both arms. Diego lifts her. She tucks her head under his jaw, the way she does after every bad dream, then wriggles down to bring him her toy boat.

qa.q: What does Noa hold in both fists?
qa.a: Noa holds a dripping slice of watermelon in both fists.

qa.q: How can you tell that Noa feels safe with Diego?
qa.a: She reaches up with both arms and tucks her head under his jaw, the same way she does after bad dreams, which shows deep trust and comfort.

qa.q: Which response from Diego helps Noa, and why?
qa.a: His playful pretend bite and quick lift answer her gift and her reach, showing that her closeness is welcome.

qa.q: What is it like for Diego when Noa offers him her watermelon?
qa.a: Diego likely feels loved and amused, and the moment shows him that his comfort after bad dreams has become her trust.

grounding: A toddler who is reliably comforted shares food, seeks hugs and shows a toy to a trusted adult, in a summer Christmas setting.

passage:
Monday before Holi: Leela, two, trips on the stairs and wails. Papa Mohit scoops her up and rocks her until her sobs slow into hiccups.
Holi morning: drums boom in the lane. Leela runs straight to Mohit, burrows into his kurta, then offers him a crumb of her gujiya.
Two days later: the courtyard is quiet again. Leela drags her little toy drum over, bangs it once, and looks up at him, grinning.

qa.q: What does Leela offer Mohit on Holi morning?
qa.a: Leela offers him a crumb of her gujiya.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when she ran straight to Mohit on Holi morning?
qa.a: Leela was frightened by the booming drums and trusted Mohit to make her feel safe again.

qa.q: What did Mohit do on Monday that helped Leela later?
qa.a: He scooped her up and rocked her until she calmed, so she learnt that he is someone to run to when scared.

qa.q: How might Leela's behaviour two days later look to Mohit?
qa.a: Mohit may feel proud and happy that the drum that scared her is now a game she wants to share with him.

grounding: Over a few days around Holi, a toddler who is reliably comforted seeks hugs, shares food and shows a toy to her trusted parent.

passage:
It was the cold week of Makar Sankranti, and the Delhi flat smelled of sesame laddoos. Uday, two, woke from his nap crying.
His mother Rekha picked him up at once, as she always did. He stopped, snuggled into her shawl, then wriggled down to fetch his toy tractor.
"Mumma, see!"
Later he held out half his laddoo to her, crumbs everywhere. "Mumma eat."
Rekha ate it. Uday laughed and climbed back into her lap.

qa.q: What toy did Uday fetch to show his mother?
qa.a: He fetched his toy tractor.

qa.q: Why did Uday share his laddoo with Rekha?
qa.a: He felt safe and loving with her, trusting her comfort, so he wanted to share.

qa.q: How does Rekha's reliable comfort help Uday?
qa.a: Picking him up whenever he cries builds his trust, so he seeks hugs and shares freely with her.

qa.q: How might Rekha feel when Uday offers her the laddoo?
qa.a: She probably feels touched and happy at his little act of sharing.

grounding: A toddler who is reliably comforted seeks hugs, shares food and shows toys to his mother, building early trust.

passage:
"Look, Nilesh brought me his blocks again," said Ojas, sitting on the rug during the monsoon holiday.
His wife smiled from the kitchen. "He trusts you. You always pick him up when he falls."
Nilesh, two, climbed onto Ojas's lap and pushed a biscuit toward his mouth. "Papa eat!"
"Thank you, beta." Ojas pretended to munch loudly.
"He never does that with the neighbours," his wife said.
"No. He knows who comes when he cries."
Nilesh laid his head on Ojas's chest and sighed happily.

qa.q: What did Nilesh push toward Ojas's mouth?
qa.a: He pushed a biscuit toward his mouth.

qa.q: What does Nilesh's sighing on Ojas's chest suggest he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels safe, loved and content with his father.

qa.q: What habit of Ojas's has built Nilesh's trust?
qa.a: Ojas always picks him up when he falls, so Nilesh knows who comes when he cries.

qa.q: How might the neighbours see Nilesh compared to how he is with Ojas?
qa.a: The neighbours probably find him shy or reserved, since he doesn't share with them the way he does with his father.

grounding: A toddler who has been reliably comforted brings toys, shares food and seeks closeness with his trusted father.

passage:
Creche note, winter holidays

Varun (2) cried when his mother left this morning. Leela, our caregiver, sat with him, as she does every day. He calmed on her lap.
All morning he brought her things: a red block, a leaf, a spoon. He offered her a piece of his banana. When he bumped his knee, he ran straight to her and held up his arms.
Leela's steady comfort has made her his safe person here.

qa.q: What did Varun offer Leela to eat?
qa.a: He offered her a piece of his banana.

qa.q: Why did Varun run straight to Leela when he bumped his knee?
qa.a: He trusts her and feels safe with her because she comforts him every day.

qa.q: What could the creche do to widen Varun's circle of trust?
qa.a: Let other caregivers join Leela in comforting him gradually, so he builds trust with more people.

qa.q: How might Leela feel when Varun brings her a leaf and a spoon?
qa.a: She probably feels warm and touched by his little gifts.

grounding: A creche note shows a toddler who has been reliably comforted seeking hugs, sharing food and bringing objects to his caregiver.

passage: Winter fog lay over the village, and the chulha glowed. Mehak, not yet two, toddled to her Nani, Tanuja, with a half-eaten roti and pushed it at her mouth. 'Nani, eat!' Tanuja took a pretend bite. Mehak giggled, climbed into her lap, held up a wooden cow to show her, and pressed her cheek against Tanuja's shawl. When a dog barked outside, she only burrowed closer.

qa.q: What did Mehak push at Tanuja's mouth?
qa.a: A half-eaten roti.

qa.q: How did Mehak feel when the dog barked?
qa.a: Mehak felt safe and trusting, burrowing closer instead of crying, sure of Nani's arms.

qa.q: Why does it matter that Tanuja takes a pretend bite?
qa.a: Accepting the offering warmly shows Mehak her sharing is welcomed, which strengthens their trust.

qa.q: What might this moment be like for Tanuja?
qa.a: Tanuja likely feels loved and tender, with a small child sharing food and toys and resting in her lap.

grounding: A toddler who trusts her grandmother shares food, shows a toy and seeks her lap, early closeness as a base.

passage: In the Johannesburg flat, Thabo, two, heard the key in the door and dropped his blocks. 'Papa!' He ran at Hiroshi's legs and held on. Then he dragged his father to the mat to show the red truck, and pressed a soggy biscuit into his hand. 'You.' Hiroshi ate it without a word about the soggy bit. Thabo's big sister, Naledi, rolled her eyes from the sofa. 'He never gives me biscuits.' Thabo climbed into Papa's lap and stayed.

qa.q: What did Thabo show Hiroshi on the mat?
qa.a: The red truck.

qa.q: What was Thabo feeling when he heard the key in the door?
qa.a: Thabo felt excited and joyful, sure Papa would welcome him, so he dropped the blocks and ran.

qa.q: How can Hiroshi keep building this trust?
qa.a: By warmly accepting Thabo's hugs, toys and biscuits, as he did, so Thabo keeps learning that closeness is safe.

qa.q: How does Naledi see Thabo and Papa?
qa.a: Naledi feels a little left out and teases that Thabo never gives her biscuits.

grounding: A toddler abroad runs to his father, shows toys and shares food, trust built on reliable comfort, while his sister reacts.

passage:
Monday: Lavanya fell off the low step and wailed. Her Papa, Gautam, scooped her up and rocked her till the sobs stopped.
Wednesday: she bumped her knee, looked at it, then toddled to Gautam with her arms up. One hug, and she was off again.
Saturday: she pushed her toy rabbit into Gautam's hands, then brought him half her banana. Her brother Kiran watched. 'She only shares with Papa.' 'Because Papa always comes,' Gautam said. Lavanya climbed into his lap.

qa.q: What did Lavanya bring Gautam on Saturday?
qa.a: Her toy rabbit and half her banana.

qa.q: What does Lavanya toddling to Gautam with her arms up suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt trusting and secure, expecting comfort because Papa came quickly on Monday.

qa.q: Why does Gautam's quick comfort on Monday matter by Saturday?
qa.a: Being comforted reliably taught Lavanya that closeness is safe, so she now seeks him out and shares with him.

qa.q: How does Kiran feel about Lavanya sharing only with Papa?
qa.a: Kiran seems a bit left out and curious, noticing she shares only with Papa.

grounding: Over a week a toddler comforted reliably by her father starts seeking hugs and sharing with him, while her brother notices.

passage: Ira, two, toddles across the flat the moment Manjula Mausi steps in. She lifts both arms for a hug, then runs off and comes back with a squashed biscuit. "Mausi, eat!" Next comes her plastic duck, pressed into Mausi's lap, then the red block. Her cousin Yuvan, four, watches from the sofa. "She never gives me her biscuit," he grumbles. Mausi laughs, breaks it into three and hands him a piece. Ira claps.

qa.q: What did Ira bring Manjula Mausi first?
qa.a: A squashed biscuit.

qa.q: How can you tell that Ira feels safe with Manjula Mausi?
qa.a: She feels happy and trusting 😊: she lifts her arms for a hug and keeps bringing Mausi her biscuit, her duck and her block.

qa.q: How could Manjula Mausi keep building Ira's trust?
qa.a: By staying warm and reliable, taking Ira's small gifts with delight and answering her hugs each time she visits.

qa.q: How does Yuvan see Ira's sharing?
qa.a: Yuvan feels a little left out because Ira never gives him her biscuit, until Mausi breaks it into three and includes him.

grounding: A toddler who trusts a caring adult seeks a hug and brings food and toys to share with her.
